catalog_quote: There are three indications that the original stress system in Umpithamu must have been one that was left-aligned, with a leftmost stress rule. The first indication is local, relating to Umpithamu’s closest relatives. Most other Middle Paman languages for which we have a reliable description of word stress have a system of this kind: this is the case, for instance, in Wik Mungkan (Kilham 1974), Kugu Nganhcara (Smith & Johnson 2000), Wik Ngathan (Sutton 1978) and possibly also Umpila (Thompson 1988). || [Blevins 2025: 142] One of these is Kugu Nganhcara, a Pama-Nyungan language of Australia, as described by Smith & Johnson (2000). In this language, with consonants /p, t, t̪, c, k, b, d, d̪, j, g, m, n, n̪, ɲ, ŋ, l, r, w, j/, all consonants except the tap, /r/, have geminate allophones optionally in intervocalic position following a short initial stressed syllable.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Kugu Nganhcara (the language of which Kugu Ugbanh is one patrilect) is reported, on the authority of Smith & Johnson 2000, to have a left-aligned word-stress system with primary stress assigned by a leftmost rule, i.e. on the word-initial syllable. Corroborated second-hand by Blevins 2025:142, who (also from Smith & Johnson 2000) describes optional gemination of intervocalic consonants 'following a short initial stressed syllable'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing reported second-hand for Kugu Nganhcara (Verstraete notes only generically that some Pama-Nyungan descriptions report alternating secondary stress).
new_statements.exceptions: None in the second-hand reports. Evans 1995 (snippet) adds that Kugu-Nganhcara is syllable-timed rather than stress-timed.
new_statements.domain_note: Word stress (Verstraete: 'description of word stress'); no information on phrase-level prominence or enclitic behaviour beyond Sutton & Hale 2021's general remark that Wik dependent pronominals are atonic.
new_statements.identity_note: All statements concern 'Kugu Nganhcara' (WALS knc; Smith & Johnson's cover term for six mutually intelligible patrilects: Kugu Muminh [kuku1283], Kugu Uwanh, Kugu Ugbanh [kuku1281, ISO ugb], Kugu Mu'inh [kuku1282], Kugu Mangk [kuku1280], Wik-Iyanh/Yi'anh [wiki1239]). Smith & Johnson 1986:34-35 (held by the project) state the patrilects 'are identical in syntax and differ in only minor aspects of their morphology and phonology', listing Ugbanh among them, so a Kugu Nganhcara stress statement is intended to cover Kuku-Ugbanh; no source describes Ugbanh prosody separately.
